title: Plato's Atlantis located in Antarctica

tellings.quote: >> Well we have a world ocean. It's where the Pacific Ocean, the Atlantic Ocean and the Indian Ocean meet. >> Sure. >> In the coastline of Antarctica.

the combatants on the other side were commanded by the kings of Atlantis, which, as I was saying, was an island greater in extent than Libya and Asia, and when afterwards sunk by an earthquake, became an impassable barrier of mud to voyagers sailing from hence to any part of the ocean.

This power came forth out of the Atlantic Ocean, for in those days the Atlantic was navigable; and there was an island situated in front of the straits which are by you called the Pillars of Heracles; the island was larger than Libya and Asia put together, and was the way to other islands, and from these you might pass to the whole of the opposite continent which surrounded the true ocean; for this sea which is within the Straits of Heracles is only a harbour, having a narrow entrance, but that other is a real sea, and the surrounding land may be most truly called a boundless continent.

related.note: Same subject (where Plato's Atlantis was) but places it in Antarctica rather than on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a competing claim.

plain: Plato's Atlantis lay on the coast of Antarctica, by the "world ocean" where the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans meet. A philosopher named Jason Jorjani puts this to Michels as his reading of Plato's dialogues the Timaeus and the Critias, and if true it would put the lost civilisation under the southern ice. In Benjamin Jowett's English translation of the Timaeus, the power of Atlantis "came forth out of the Atlantic Ocean" from an island "in front of the straits which are by you called the Pillars of Heracles", the ancient name for the mouth of the Mediterranean, beyond which lay "the opposite continent which surrounded the true ocean"; the text names no southern continent and no meeting of three oceans.

discussion.text: In Jowett's translation of the Timaeus, the power of Atlantis "came forth out of the Atlantic Ocean" from an island "in front of the straits which are by you called the Pillars of Heracles", from which "you might pass to the whole of the opposite continent which surrounded the true ocean"; the text sets the island itself in the Atlantic before the straits, with that continent beyond it. Reading "the opposite continent" or "the true ocean" as Antarctica and the world ocean around it, and placing Atlantis there, is the teller's step, which the text neither states nor excludes.
